accepted_phrases: Separate contact construction from downstream detection. In a membrane keyboard, pressing brings conductive layers together, bridges a normally open gap, allows current to flow, and lets the parent device register a keypress. In a keyboard matrix, the controller scans columns and rows, identifies the pressed row-column intersection, and generates the corresponding code from a binary switch state. The material explains these stages but contains no controlled membrane-versus-mechanical latency or accuracy trial, so it does not prove that every mechanical keyboard registers faster or makes every user more accurate.

Keep the transition reports at individual scope. One long-time Mac-like and Logitech Craft user has not tried a mechanical keyboard and asks about quietness, a numpad, no soldering, cross-platform support, and accuracy expectations. One Cherry MX Brown user reports less tactility than their laptop and membrane Logitech K120 and demands a force chart before buying. A first-time mechanical-board builder reports excellent Tealio linear feel but also an overly sensitive W switch that required desoldering and replacement. Together these accounts show configuration and person dependence; they are neither a controlled comparison nor evidence of population prevalence or a universal mechanical advantage.

Within the documented Cherry MX family, Red is linear, Brown is tactile non-clicky, and Blue is tactile clicky; force and actuation behavior vary by switch type. The source says Cherry MX switches are often referenced by stem color, while other makers may use Cherry switches or imitate them, and it records linear, tactile, and clicky Grey variants. The catalog examples separately use OUTEMU, unspecified, and Gateron labels, including Gateron Yellow, Orange, and Pink, while a community switch database reports missing Gateron and smaller manufacturers. Therefore switch colors are not a cross-manufacturer universal standard, and the behavior of every switch cannot be inferred from color alone. Verify the exact manufacturer, family, model, specifications, sound, and feel.

Treat the four catalog pages as configuration snapshots rather than independent tests. The 34.99 dollar example advertises a wired 68-key blue-switch configuration. The 89.99 dollar example advertises a wired 61-key hot-swappable board with Gateron Yellow, Orange, or Pink options. The 49.99 dollar HYSSP example advertises 61 keys, Bluetooth and USB-C, brown or blue styles, and no posted review. The 49.99 dollar NEWMEN example advertises a full-size 104-key USB hot-swappable OUTEMU board with red or blue styles. Compare exact needed keys and layout, connection and operating-system support, room-noise limit, switch maker and model, force and feedback, hot-swap or soldering tolerance, price, and return terms. Try a switch sample when possible, then test the complete board during sustained typing because layout, case, plate, keycaps, stabilizers, firmware, and connection behavior remain board-level properties.

Explain the contact-to-controller registration chain and the Cherry MX Red, Brown, and Blue shorthand with an explicit manufacturer boundary. Do not promise that mechanical is universally faster, more accurate, quieter, more tactile, or better, and do not infer every switch from color. Treat seller pages as snapshots and community reports as scoped experiences. Select a returnable exact configuration only after its layout, connectivity, noise, switch maker and model, hot-swap, and budget fit the buyer and after a switch sample and complete-board trial where possible; otherwise keep the current keyboard or defer.

Explain the registration chain, scope color meanings to the exact switch family, and use a returnable exact-configuration trial against the buyer's layout, connection, noise, feel, hot-swap, and budget needs; if exact switch or complete-board testing is unavailable, keep the current keyboard or defer without naming a universal winner.
Use manufacturer-specific switch evidence and a complete-board trial, not a cross-brand color shortcut, seller rating, or universal mechanical-better claim.

The frozen material supports membrane contact closure, keyboard-matrix detection, Cherry MX family categories, four seller configurations, and conflicting individual experiences, but it lacks a controlled membrane-versus-mechanical performance comparison, a cross-manufacturer color standard, and this buyer's switch-sample or complete-board trial.

Physical contact closure or switch state and downstream matrix scanning and keycode generation are distinct stages, so feel or mechanism labels alone do not establish universal registration speed or accuracy.

Red, Brown, and Blue have the documented linear, tactile non-clicky, and tactile clicky meanings only within the cited Cherry MX family; colors are not a cross-manufacturer universal standard and cannot identify every switch's behavior.

Catalog pages establish listing-level layouts, connection modes, switch labels, hot-swap claims, prices, and ratings, while forum pages establish only individual requirements and experiences; neither source role supplies a controlled universal quality or outcome ranking.

A switch sample can narrow feel preferences, but a returnable complete-board trial is needed for layout, noise, stabilized keys, firmware, connection behavior, and sustained typing, and the purchase result remains specific to that configuration and user.
Every mechanical keyboard registers faster than every membrane keyboard and automatically improves every user's accuracy.
A modern membrane keyboard cannot provide any tactile feedback because it has no mechanical switch.
Switch color is a universal cross-manufacturer standard, so every red, brown, blue, yellow, orange, or pink switch has the same behavior.
The Cherry MX Red, Brown, and Blue mapping is enough to infer the exact behavior of Gateron, OUTEMU, and every unspecified switch with the same or another color.
The Brown and Tealio forum reports establish how most users will experience membrane and mechanical keyboards.
The listing prices, ratings, and feature claims independently prove which board has the best quality, durability, typing speed, and latency.
Liking one loose switch sample proves that every complete keyboard using that label will fit the buyer during sustained typing.
Choose one of the four catalog keyboards as the universal first-board winner without exact switch, layout, connection, noise, return, or complete-board testing.

research_subgoals.description: Explain the physical contact-to-controller registration chain, separating membrane contact closure from row-column scanning and keycode generation without making an unsupported speed or accuracy comparison.
Explain the documented Cherry MX Red, Brown, and Blue categories and prove why color cannot be treated as a cross-manufacturer universal standard across the listed switch makers and configurations.
Reconcile the untried first-buyer question, negative Brown report, and positive Tealio report with its unit caveat while preserving individual rather than prevalence scope.
Compare the four listing-level configurations and combine mechanism, color scope, and experience evidence into an exact-switch and complete-board trial process with a bounded defer option.

query_requirements.text: Explain how a press becomes a registered keycode by separating membrane contact closure, binary switch state, matrix scanning, and row-column code generation, and state why this material cannot establish a universal mechanical speed or accuracy advantage.

Describe Red, Brown, and Blue only as documented Cherry MX family categories, explicitly state that switch colors are not a cross-manufacturer universal standard, and explain why exact behavior cannot be inferred for every OUTEMU, Gateron, unspecified, or other switch from color alone.

Use the long-time nonmechanical user's constraints, the negative Cherry MX Brown report, and the positive Tealio report with its sensitive-switch caveat as scoped experiences and disagreement, not a controlled comparison or prevalence estimate.

Compare the four seller snapshots across layout, connection, exact switch maker and label, hot-swap, price, and review status without ranking quality, then give a switch-sample and return-window complete-board checklist for noise, required keys, shortcuts, simultaneous inputs, connectivity, firmware, and sustained typing; select conditionally or defer rather than naming a universal winner.
